Barycentric

GeometryCoordinatesAlgebra
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and the point P, and watch three lines cut the opposite sides into pieces.
How to play: Drag a dot with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show names, P's three numbers and the numbers on the sides.
2
Look for the math

Three numbers can describe a point inside a triangle: they are the weights you would hang at the three corners to make the triangle balance at that point. The applet shows how the very same three numbers turn up on the sides when you draw lines through the point.

Three weights, one balance point

Give the corners A, B and C the weights α, β, γ. Their center of mass is

P = (αA + βB + γC) / (α + β + γ)

Because only the ratios matter, we may choose α + β + γ = 1. These are the barycentric coordinates of P. The numbers beside P in this picture are exactly that normalized triple: the logic test checks at 300 interior and 240 exterior positions that they add to 1 and that putting those weights at the corners lands back on P. Move P outside the triangle and two of the numbers become negative — the formula still works.

Where a cevian lands

Write P using the first equation with α + β + γ = 1:

P = αA + (β + γ)[(β/(β+γ))B + (γ/(β+γ))C]

The expression in brackets is a point on BC. It is A', where the line AP meets BC, and it is the balance point of just the weights at B and C. Rearranging gives β(A' − B) = γ(C − A'), so

BA' / A'C = γ / β

The same argument at the other two corners gives all three side splits in the article. The logic test checks each against the distances along the sides, including points outside the triangle where the ratios are negative.

Read the ratios from the sides

The article states, and the test confirms at every one of the 300 interior positions:

BA'/A'C = γ/β,  CB'/B'A = α/γ,  AC'/C'B = β/α

Multiply them and everything cancels: (γ/β)(α/γ)(β/α) = 1, which is Ceva's theorem — the reason the three lines through P really do meet at one point. The three mode buttons print these numbers the way the applet does: Inherited shows the weights β, γ belonging to the two ends of the side; Add to 1 shows the two pieces of the side as γ/(β+γ) and β/(β+γ), which sum to 1; A la Routh shows β/γ and 1. The test compares all 15 digit settings and all three modes with the applet's own drawing code.

From side ratios back to P

Go the other way. Suppose the sides are cut so that BA'/A'C = λ, CB'/B'A = μ, AC'/C'B = ν, with λμν = 1. The article sets β = 1; then γ = λ and α = λμ, so

P = (λμ, 1, λ) = (μ, μν, 1) = (1, ν, λν)

These are the triples that appear in Routh's theorem; here the Ceva condition makes them describe the same point. The logic test tries 1,600 pairs of ratio values, reconstructs P from all three triples and checks that each point's own side ratios return λ, μ and ν.

Try pulling P just outside the triangle: one coordinate turns negative, and the side numbers follow it.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
